title: Trump Replaces Expiring Global Tariffs With New 10-12.5% Duties on 60 Trading Partners
excerpt: India faces a 10% levy under Section 301 as the administration pivots from struck-down reciprocal tariffs to forced-labor enforcement, covering 99.4% of U.S. imports.
body:
• The Trump administration imposed new tariffs of 10% and 12.5% on goods from 60 trading partners on Friday, replacing a temporary 10% global levy that expired at midnight.
  • India faces a 10% tariff — down from an initially proposed 12.5% — after amending its foreign trade policy in June to ban forced-labor imports; Indian textile exporters warn of disadvantage against rivals.
  • Markets largely shrugged off the move, with analysts noting the new structure broadly mirrors existing tariff levels but places them on firmer legal footing under Section 301.

The United States on Friday imposed new tariffs on goods from 60 trading partners, replacing a temporary 10% global levy that expired at 12:01 a.m. EDT with duties of 10% and 12.5% that cover 99.4% of all U.S. imports, according to Reuters.

The move is the White House's first step in rebuilding President Donald Trump's near-global tariff wall after the U.S. Supreme Court in February struck down his "reciprocal" tariffs of 10% to 50%, which had been imposed under a national emergencies law to shrink the trade deficit. A temporary 10% tariff under Section 122 of the Trade Act served as a bridge; the new duties, issued under Section 301 of the same act, are designed to withstand future legal challenges.

How the Rates Break Down

Seventeen economies, including India, Canada, Mexico, the United Kingdom, Bangladesh, Indonesia and Pakistan, will face a 10% tariff. The U.S. Trade Representative said these countries have adopted — or taken steps to adopt — bans on imports produced with forced labor.

The remaining 43 trading partners, including China, Vietnam and others that lack comparable provisions, face a 12.5% rate. The European Union, Taiwan, Japan, South Korea and Switzerland were assigned rates that, combined with existing most-favored-nation duties, total 10% or 12.5%, in line with prior trade deal commitments.

"The United States has had a forced labor import ban for nearly a century, and rigorously enforces it. It's well past time for our trading partners to do the same."

— Jamieson Greer, U.S. Trade Representative

Numerous products are exempt, including oil and gas, fertilizer, certain foodstuffs, aircraft, critical minerals and goods already subject to Section 232 national security tariffs on autos, steel, aluminum and copper.

India's Exposure

India's 10% rate is lower than the 12.5% initially proposed in June, after New Delhi amended its foreign trade policy on June 14, 2026, to prohibit imports of goods produced using forced labor, according to the Outlook Business report. The U.S. Trade Representative acknowledged the policy change in its final determination.

Still, Indian exporters face headwinds. The Confederation of Indian Textile Industry warned Friday that India was excluded from new tariff-rate quotas allowing textile and apparel shipments from Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia and Malaysia — using U.S.-origin cotton — to enter the U.S. duty-free, according to Reuters. India's textile and apparel exports to the U.S. are worth nearly $11 billion annually.

"The differential treatment risks diverting sourcing orders for textile and apparel items away from India," CITI Chairman Ashwin Chandran said. Ajay Srivastava of the Global Trade Research Initiative estimated about 70% of Indian exports to the U.S. — including garments, machinery, chemicals and gems — would face regular duties plus the new levy.

Market Reaction and Global Response

Wall Street largely shrugged. Jim Reid of Deutsche Bank said the new structure "broadly mirrors the tariff levels that markets were already operating under." Goldman Sachs chief economist Jan Hatzius said the overall U.S. effective tariff rate should be "little changed," according to Barron's.

Bond yields edged higher as the tariffs added to inflation risk, but reaction was generally limited in financial markets more focused on the Middle East conflict, Reuters reported.

Trading partners pushed back on the forced-labor justification, though several noted the practical impact was muted. The European Union said the outcome was "in line with U.S. tariff commitments" from their joint statement and provided "positive momentum" for further negotiations. Britain said its trade agreement was unaffected, with zero tariffs on whisky and medical technology confirmed.

China said it opposed all unilateral tariffs. Australia, Brazil and Norway called the new levies unjustified and said they would seek removal.

What Comes Next

Analysts said the focus will shift to exemptions, country-specific negotiations and a second Section 301 investigation into excess industrial capacity targeting 16 trading partners, including the EU, China, India, Japan and South Korea. For India, the tariffs add pressure as Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal and Greer negotiate Phase 1 of a bilateral trade agreement. New Delhi is seeking to preserve its comparative advantage over regional competitors in the final arrangement.

The tariffs took effect Friday, with goods in transit exempted until July 28 at 12:01 a.m. EDT.
image_caption: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and U.S. President Donald Trump at a bilateral meeting. India faces a 10% tariff under the new Section 301 trade action covering 60 U.S. trading partners.
nri_angle: Indian textile and apparel exports worth $11 billion annually face new competitive pressure, with India excluded from duty-free quotas granted to regional rivals.
